title: The bond market is signaling trouble ahead. This is why you should pay attention
summary:
It's a simple rule: Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions from each other.
If bond prices are rising, investors are fine getting less in interest since they are holding bonds that are appreciating in value.
Rising bond yields can also push up interest rates on credit cards, car loans — and all kinds of borrowing costs across the economy.
And, obviously, rising bond yields impact how much the government itself has to pay in interest.
In other words, bond investors and stock investors tend to see things differently.

title: Scott Bessent on the national debt: ‘There’s nothing magic about the $40 trillion number’
summary:
The U.S. national debt crossed $40 trillion for the first time this week, but Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent wants Americans—and markets—to shrug it off.
"There's nothing magic about the $40 trillion number," Bessent told CNBC's Sara Eisen in an exclusive interview on Squawk on the Street Thursday.
What is Treasury Secretary Bessent's strategy for the $40 trillion debt?
The gross national debt crossed the $40 trillion mark, according to Treasury Department data, just five months after hitting $39 trillion in March.

title: Bessent’s Plan at Best ‘Circuit Breaker’ for Global Bond Slump
summary:
(Bloomberg) -- The global bond rally triggered by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's plan to increase buybacks of longer-dated debt may prove short lived, with analysts citing persistent worries about fiscal woes and sticky inflation globally.
Led by the extended declines in 30-year and 10-year Treasury yields from multi-decade highs, government debt markets across Asia Pacific, from Japan to Australia, powered ahead in tandem on Thursday.
"It's going to be a circuit breaker for this long-end selloff globally," said Andrew Lilley, chief rates strategist at Barrenjoey Markets Pty in Sydney.
For one, Franklin Templeton maintains underweight on long-maturity bonds, arguing that Bessent's move is unlikely to spark a more sustained rally.
"I can't see the longer end finding too much of a bid as long as those forces are prevailing."

title: Economic adviser O'Neill rules out government job but urges boldness on devolution
summary:
Economist Lord Jim O'Neill, who has been advising the prime minister, has said he will not be taking a job in Andy Burnham's government.
The former chief economist at Goldman Sachs had been tipped to become Burnham's chief economic adviser.
He noted that the country has boosted government spending "dramatically" in recent years and needed a "more sensible approach to welfare spending under genuine welfare reform".
From 2015-2016, Lord O'Neill was commercial secretary to the Treasury under the then-Chancellor, George Osborne.
Lord O'Neill is also known as the economist who coined the term Bric in 2001 to describe leading developing or newly industrialised countries with potential for fast growth and, therefore, investment returns.

title: Paul Atkins Misreads Adam Smith and the American Founding
summary:
Jefferson may have encountered Smith’s ideas before 1776, but there is no evidence that “The Wealth of Nations” shaped the Declaration.
That missing half of the founding tradition becomes impossible to ignore when Mr. Atkins turns to cryptocurrency.
Mr. Atkins’s crypto agenda is difficult to reconcile with his tribute to Adam Smith, because Smith did not regard money and banking as a realm beyond public law.
If Mr. Atkins is looking for a lesson about socialism, he might begin with the history of the agency he leads.
Mr. Atkins wants the founders to bless a world in which public power retreats and private financial power is presumed innocent.

title: Foreign tariffs made US whiskey cheaper in some places
summary:
University North Carolina State UniversityA new study finds that one side effect of Trump-era trade wars has been cheaper whiskey in much of the United States.
In 2018, the Trump administration imposed a series of tariffs, kicking off a trade war with many prominent trade partners.
In response, Mexico, the European Union, Canada, and China imposed substantial tariffs on whiskey produced in the US.
“Overall, US whiskey producers responded to export tariffs by decreasing the cost of whiskey in order to increase domestic sales,” says Burd.
That means whiskey producers couldn’t respond to decreased exports in 2018 by quickly scaling back production.
